import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 189

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/189](https://www.erdosproblems.com/189)
-/

open Affine EuclideanGeometry

namespace Erdos189

/-- Erdős problem 189 asked whether the below holds for all rectangles. -/
def Erdos189For (P : ℝ² → ℝ² → ℝ² → ℝ² → Prop) (A : ℝ² → ℝ² → ℝ² → ℝ² → ℝ) :=
    ∀ᵉ (n > 0) (colouring : ℝ² → Fin n), ∃ colour, ∀ area > (0 : ℝ), ∃ a b c d,
      {a, b, c, d} ⊆ colouring⁻¹' {colour} ∧
      IsCcwConvexPolygon ![a, b, c, d] ∧
      A a b c d = area ∧
      P a b c d

/--
If $\mathbb{R}^2$ is finitely coloured then must there exist some colour class which contains the
vertices of a rectangle of every area?

Graham, "On Partitions of 𝔼ⁿ", Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series A 28, 89-91 (1980).
(See "Concluding Remarks" on page 96.)

Solved (with answer `False`, as formalised below) in:
Vjekoslav Kovač, "Coloring and density theorems for configurations of a given volume", 2023
https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.09973
In fact, Kovač's colouring is even Jordan measurable (the topological boundary of each
monochromatic region is Lebesgue measurable and has measure zero).

This was formalized in Lean by Alexeev and Kovac using Aristotle.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5 51, formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/main/src/v4.24.0/ErdosProblems/Erdos189.lean"]
theorem erdos_189 :
    answer(False) ↔ Erdos189For
      (fun a b c d ↦
        line[ℝ, a, b].direction ⟂ line[ℝ, b, c].direction ∧
        line[ℝ, b, c].direction ⟂ line[ℝ, c, d].direction ∧
        line[ℝ, c, d].direction ⟂ line[ℝ, d, a].direction)
      (fun a b c d ↦ dist a b * dist b c) := by
  sorry

/-- Graham claims this is "easy to see". -/
@[category research solved, AMS 5 51]
theorem erdos_189.variants.square :
    ¬ Erdos189For
      (fun a b c d ↦
        line[ℝ, a, b].direction ⟂ line[ℝ, b, c].direction ∧
        line[ℝ, b, c].direction ⟂ line[ℝ, c, d].direction ∧
        line[ℝ, c, d].direction ⟂ line[ℝ, d, a].direction ∧
        dist a b = dist b c)
      (fun a b c d ↦ dist a b * dist b c) := by
  sorry

/--
Seems to be open, as of January 2025.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 5 51]
theorem erdos_189.variants.parallelogram :
    ¬ Erdos189For
      (fun a b c d ↦
        line[ℝ, a, b] ∥ line[ℝ, c, d] ∧
        line[ℝ, a, d] ∥ line[ℝ, b, c])
      (fun a b c d ↦ dist a b * dist b c * (∡ a b c).sin) := by
  sorry

end Erdos189

findings.description: The leading `¬ Erdos189For ...` selects a negative answer to the parallelogram question. The cited literature asks whether the positive property holds, without proposing its negation as a conjecture. This may be an intentional choice of conjectural direction, but it is not supported by the cited sources. The concern is the selected polarity, not the geometric predicates or the `research open` status.
findings.source_evidence: Erdős–Graham, Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number theory (1980), printed p. 15, asks whether the preceding result about one class containing configurations of every area also holds for rectangles or parallelograms (https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~ronspubs/80_11_number_theory.pdf). Kovač, arXiv:2309.09973v3, §1.3, Problem 6, explicitly asks: “If R² is finitely colored then must there exist some color-class which contains the vertices of a parallelogram of every given area?” It states that this question remains unanswered, rather than conjecturing a negative answer (https://arxiv.org/e-print/2309.09973).
findings.suggested_fix: Preserve the unresolved question by replacing the leading `¬` with `answer(sorry) ↔`, leaving the parallelogram predicate and area function unchanged. Alternatively, document and cite an intended separate negative conjecture.

findings.description: The docstring gives Graham's article page range as 89–91. The article occupies pages 89–97; the cited concluding remarks on page 96 are consequently outside the range currently given. This does not affect the mathematics.
findings.source_evidence: Graham's publication index lists “On Partitions of E^n,” Journal of Combinatorial Theory (A) 28 (1980), 89–97 (https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~ronspubs/). The article includes pages 96–97 (https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~ronspubs/80_03_partitions.pdf), and Kovač's bibliography entry Gra80 independently gives 89–97.

reformulations.difference: Rectangles are expressed using a strictly convex ordered quadrilateral and only three successive perpendicularity conditions, rather than explicitly requiring four right angles.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The convex-polygon condition excludes repeated vertices and collinear triples. Thus the three perpendicularity conditions give three genuine right interior angles. A convex quadrilateral's interior angles sum to 2π, so its fourth angle is also right. Conversely, any nondegenerate rectangle can be cyclically labelled with the orientation required by IsCcwConvexPolygon and satisfies these three conditions. The product of adjacent side lengths is its ordinary area. Adding equality of the adjacent lengths, as the square variant does, gives precisely a square.

reformulations.difference: The area function uses the sine of an oriented angle without an absolute value.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: IsCcwConvexPolygon ![a,b,c,d] implies `(∡ a b c).sign = 1`. Mathlib defines this sign as the sign of the sine, so that sine is strictly positive. The oriented angle's real representative lies in (0,π) and equals the corresponding unoriented interior angle. Consequently the given expression equals `dist a b * dist b c * Real.sin (∠ a b c)`, the ordinary parallelogram area. In scratch.lean, signed_area_formulation_iff proves the equivalence of the complete Erdos189For statements using these two area functions, for arbitrary P.

review.notes: Checked all four declarations, quantifier scopes, colour-class membership, positive-area restrictions, and the relevant geometry definitions. Scratch proofs establish distinctness of all four vertices, positivity of the parallelogram area, and the oriented/unoriented area equivalence. Concrete unit-square and slanted-parallelogram tests pass. The linked rectangle proof was checked after three local compatibility edits; its final theorem depends only on propext, Classical.choice, and Quot.sound. Its negative conclusion and Graham's negative square result agree with the recorded solved statuses. Kovač's January 2026 revision still records the parallelogram question as open. The live erdosproblems.com/189 page remained blocked by Cloudflare despite descriptive User-Agent requests, so later website status updates could not be checked; the mathematical wording was verified from the primary literature instead. The reviewed file remains byte-for-byte identical to the supplied commit.
